### 68_doc_application_web_aiJcwfService_h

<a id="68-doc-application-web-aijcwfservice-h"></a>

*Source doc:* `../../../queue/jarvisCppSafetyAudit/68_doc_application_web_aiJcwfService_h/docu.output.md`



### [CRITICAL] `this` captured by raw pointer in detached background threads; `Shutdown()` joins under the mutex that `Broadcast()` also locks — potential deadlock

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `AiJcwfService::Shutdown()`, `AiJcwfService::ExplainAsync()`, `AiJcwfService::GenerateAsync()`, `AiJcwfService::FixFailedScriptAsync()` (~lines spanning the thread-launch and shutdown regions)
- **Issue:** `Shutdown()` acquires `m_ThreadsMutex` and then calls `thread.join()` on every background thread. Each background thread, while running, calls `Broadcast()` which acquires `m_BroadcastMutex`. But if the same thread also ever tries to call back into `JoinFinishedThreads()` or any code path that grabs `m_ThreadsMutex` while `Shutdown()` holds it, a deadlock forms. More concretely: the entire `join()` loop runs *inside* the `m_ThreadsMutex` lock. Any code path in the background lambda that takes `m_ThreadsMutex` (e.g., a future call to `JoinFinishedThreads` if it were ever un-stubbed, or if `ExplainAsync`/`GenerateAsync` are called concurrently from another thread while `Shutdown` is running) will deadlock. The join-under-lock pattern is the root cause.
- **Impact:** If `Shutdown()` is called while another thread calls `ExplainAsync()` (which also locks `m_ThreadsMutex` to push a thread), the two lock acquisitions on `m_ThreadsMutex` serialise correctly, but `join()` inside the lock means no new requests can be accepted and no housekeeping can proceed until all threads finish — threads that may themselves be waiting on `m_BroadcastMutex`. If `Broadcast` is ever called synchronously from the destructor path this becomes a guaranteed deadlock.
- **Fix:** Release the mutex before joining. Snapshot the thread vector under the lock, clear it, then join outside:
  ```
  std::vector<std::thread> toJoin;
  { std::lock_guard lk(m_ThreadsMutex); toJoin.swap(m_BackgroundThreads); }
  for (auto& t : toJoin) if (t.joinable()) t.join();
  ```

---

### [CRITICAL] `this` reference captured into background threads with no lifetime guarantee

- **Category:** lifetime / concurrency
- **Location:** `ExplainAsync`, `GenerateAsync`, `FixFailedScriptAsync` — lambda captures `[this, ...]`
- **Issue:** Each background thread lambda captures `this` by raw pointer. Nothing prevents the `AiJcwfService` object from being destroyed while a background thread is still running. `Shutdown()` is supposed to prevent this, but it is only called from the destructor; any caller who destroys the object without calling `Shutdown()` first (or who catches an exception from a higher-level constructor after `AiJcwfService` was fully constructed) will leave running threads that access freed memory. The lambdas also capture local `std::string` values that were moved into the lambda closure correctly, but they subsequently call `Broadcast`, `RunSingleAiCall`, and access `m_ShuttingDown`, `m_NextRequestSeq` etc. — all through the dangling `this`.
- **Impact:** Use-after-free crash on any uncontrolled destruction path.
- **Fix:** Wrap `AiJcwfService` itself in `shared_ptr` at the ownership site and capture `weak_ptr<AiJcwfService>` in each lambda, locking it at the top of the thread body. Alternatively enforce that `Shutdown()` is always called before destruction (add an `assert(!m_BackgroundThreads.empty() || m_ShuttingDown)` in the destructor or use `std::jthread` with a stop token).

---

### [HIGH] `std::promise` set from a curl callback thread after the `std::future` has timed out — `set_value` on an already-abandoned shared state causes `std::future_error`

- **Category:** concurrency / exception
- **Location:** `AiJcwfService::RunSingleAiCall`, around the `future.wait_for` / `promise->set_value` block
- **Issue:** When `future.wait_for` returns `std::future_status::timeout`, `RunSingleAiCall` returns `false`. The `AiRequestPool` callback lambda still holds a `shared_ptr<std::promise<AiReply>>` and will call `promise->set_value(reply)` when the AI eventually responds. At that point the future is already destroyed (it went out of scope on the `RunSingleAiCall` stack). Calling `set_value` on a promise whose future has been destroyed is well-defined only if the promise is then itself destroyed — but calling `set_value` after the future is gone will throw `std::future_error` with `std::future_errc::no_state` or `broken_promise` depending on destruction order. The callback lambda running on the curl I/O thread or pool thread will throw an uncaught exception on that thread, terminating the process.
- **Impact:** Process termination on slow AI calls that exceed `AI_CALL_TIMEOUT_MS`.
- **Fix:** Guard `set_value` with a try/catch in the callback lambda, or use `promise->set_value` only if the future has not yet been abandoned. A cleaner design uses an `std::atomic<bool> cancelled` flag shared between the wait side and the callback, so the callback becomes a no-op when the caller has moved on.

---

### [HIGH] `ResolveJcwfInterfaceName()` dereferences `Core::g_Core` without null check; `TestAiInterface` and `RunSingleAiCall` call functions on `Core::g_Core` after a prior null check only in `RunSingleAiCall`

- **Category:** memory / lifetime
- **Location:** `ResolveJcwfInterfaceName()` (anonymous namespace); `TestAiInterface` (~line using `Core::g_Core->GetConfig()`)
- **Issue:** `ResolveJcwfInterfaceName` reads `Core::g_Core->GetConfig()` with no null guard. It is called from `RunSingleAiCall`, which does check `Core::g_Core == nullptr` earlier, but `ResolveJcwfInterfaceName` is a static free function that can be called independently. `TestAiInterface` also reads `Core::g_Core->GetConfig()` directly without a guard (it checks `interfaceIndex >= config.m_ApiInterfaces.size()` but never checks `Core::g_Core`).
- **Impact:** Null pointer dereference if `Core::g_Core` is torn down before background threads finish.
- **Fix:** Add `if (Core::g_Core == nullptr) return {};` at the top of `ResolveJcwfInterfaceName`. Add the same guard at the top of `TestAiInterface`.

---

### [HIGH] Background thread lambda references `broadcastResult` / `broadcastProgress` / `runValidation` / `generatedScripts` which are stack-locals — but the lambda is the thread body, so they're captured by value/reference into the closure; verify `generatedScripts` capture is by reference into `broadcastResult`

- **Category:** lifetime
- **Location:** `GenerateAsync` lambda body — `broadcastResult` captures `generatedScripts` by reference (`[&]`); `generatedScripts` is a local in the lambda's own scope
- **Issue:** `broadcastResult` is a local lambda inside the thread lambda that captures `generatedScripts` by reference (`[&]`). `generatedScripts` is itself a local variable in the enclosing (thread) lambda. This is safe as long as `broadcastResult` is never called after `generatedScripts` goes out of scope, and indeed in the current code it appears to be used only within the same scope. However, `runValidation` similarly captures `generatedJcwf` by reference from the outer lambda scope. If any future refactor moves `broadcastResult` into a longer-lived context, this becomes a dangling reference. The nested lambda-captures-local-by-reference pattern is inherently fragile.
- **Impact:** Currently latent; becomes dangling reference on refactor.
- **Fix:** Capture `generatedScripts` by value in `broadcastResult`, or restructure so `broadcastResult` takes it as a parameter. Rust's borrow checker would reject the by-reference capture the moment the referent's lifetime doesn't provably cover the closure's use. C++ equivalent: capture by value, or use `gsl::not_null` + explicit parameter passing.

---

### [HIGH] `fs::exists(sp)` followed by use — TOCTOU race on script path check

- **Category:** TOCTOU
- **Location:** `GenerateAsync` lambda, script generation loop — `if (!fs::exists(sp))`
- **Issue:** The code checks `fs::exists(sp)` and, if false, adds the script to `newScripts`. Between the check and any subsequent write (done by the front-end after the broadcast), another process or concurrent workflow run could create the file. This is a classic check-then-act race.
- **Impact:** Silent overwrite of a script that was created between the check and the write; or, conversely, a script that appears to need generation but is created externally before the AI call completes.
- **Fix:** At the write site use `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` (or `std::ios::out` with a check that the file did not previously exist). Accept that the race window is small but document it, or hold an exclusive advisory lock on the scripts directory during generation.

---

### [HIGH] `popen` result used without checking for `nullptr` in `GetHostOsDescription()` on macOS path — partial; actually checked, but `pclose` not called on empty-result path

- **Category:** resource
- **Location:** `GetHostOsDescription()`, macOS branch
- **Issue:** When `fgets` reads data but the result is empty after trimming, the function falls through to `return "macOS (version unknown)"` — but `pclose(pipe)` has already been called above in the happy path. However, examining carefully: `pclose` is called unconditionally before the `if (!result.empty())` check. This is correct for the macOS path. The real issue is that if `popen` returns non-null but the `while (fgets(...))` loop exits with `result` still empty (zero bytes read), `pclose` is still called. That part is fine. **However**, the function is called repeatedly (once per script generation, once per JCWF generation call) from background threads, spawning a subprocess each time. This is a performance issue but not a safety one per se. The actual resource issue: on a system where `sw_vers` hangs, the background thread hangs indefinitely with no timeout.
- **Impact:** Background thread indefinite block if `sw_vers` hangs; denial of progress.
- **Fix:** Cache the OS description string in a `static std::string` (computed once via `std::call_once`) to avoid repeated subprocess spawns. Add a timeout via `alarm(2)` or move to `std::filesystem`-based OS detection.

---

### [MEDIUM] `m_BackgroundThreads` grows unboundedly; threads are never removed until `Shutdown()`

- **Category:** resource / memory
- **Location:** `ExplainAsync`, `GenerateAsync`, `FixFailedScriptAsync`; `JoinFinishedThreads()` is a no-op stub
- **Issue:** `JoinFinishedThreads()` has a comment saying "Threads are joined in Shutdown(). No active cleanup needed here." but the function does nothing. Every call to `ExplainAsync` etc. appends a `std::thread` to `m_BackgroundThreads`. Completed (joinable but finished) threads are never harvested. Over time, especially if the user clicks the explain/generate buttons repeatedly, `m_BackgroundThreads` accumulates hundreds of `std::thread` objects each holding OS handles.
- **Impact:** Resource leak proportional to request count; `std::thread` destructor calls `std::terminate` if a thread is still joinable and the vector is destroyed before `Shutdown()`, which would happen if an exception unwinds the owning object.
- **Fix:** Implement `JoinFinishedThreads` to scan the vector and erase threads whose `joinable()` returns false (i.e., already joined or detached), or use a different approach: a thread pool with a bounded queue, or `std::jthread` with cooperative cancellation.

---

### [MEDIUM] `std::future` wait timeout does not cancel the in-flight AI request; the `AiRequestPool` callback still fires and calls `promise->set_value` after `future` is destroyed

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `RunSingleAiCall` — `future.wait_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(AI_CALL_TIMEOUT_MS))`
- **Issue:** This is a separate dimension of the promise/future issue above: the timeout path returns `false` from `RunSingleAiCall` but there is no mechanism to signal `AiRequestPool` to cancel the pending request. The pool will continue consuming resources (network socket, curl handle, memory for the response buffer) for the full duration of the AI provider's response, even though the caller has given up.
- **Impact:** Resource waste; accumulated in-flight requests on slow AI providers; potential for the callback thread to touch freed data if the pool itself is torn down.
- **Fix:** Add a cancellation token (e.g., `std::atomic<bool>` shared between `RunSingleAiCall` and the callback; pass it to `AiRequestPool::Submit`) that causes the callback to be a no-op and signals the pool to abort the transfer.

---

### [MEDIUM] `FindMatchingBrace` does not handle multi-byte UTF-8 sequences — a `}` byte inside a multi-byte character could be misidentified

- **Category:** memory / correctness
- **Location:** `FindMatchingBrace()` in anonymous namespace
- **Issue:** The function iterates byte-by-byte and tracks `inStr` state to skip string contents. It handles `\"` escape sequences, but not UTF-8 multi-byte sequences. A byte `0x7D` (`}`) cannot appear as a continuation byte in valid UTF-8 (continuation bytes are `0x80–0xBF`), so this is safe for valid UTF-8. However, a `"` byte (`0x22`) *can* appear as a continuation byte in overlong or malformed UTF-8 sequences. If the input JSON contains malformed UTF-8, `inStr` may toggle at the wrong point, causing `FindMatchingBrace` to return the wrong position, leading to incorrect JSON manipulation in `MergeJcwfFragments` and `PatchTasksIntoJcwf`.
- **Impact:** Incorrect JCWF JSON produced; workflow generation silently produces a malformed file.
- **Fix:** Use a proper JSON library (simdjson is already available) to locate task boundaries rather than hand-rolled brace matching.

---

### [MEDIUM] `ExtractTaskBlock` / `FindTaskBlockBounds` search for task keys by plain string `find` — can match task IDs that are substrings of other task IDs

- **Category:** correctness
- **Location:** `FindTaskBlockBounds()` — `jcwf.find(searchKey, searchStart)`
- **Issue:** `searchKey` is `"\"" + taskId + "\""`. A task with ID `"parse"` will match before `"parseSSHLog"` if the latter appears first as text. The colon-check after the key-find mitigates this for well-formed JSON (because `"parse"` followed by non-whitespace non-colon is rejected), but the loop's `searchStart = afterKey` advance may skip the real key on the retry. Additionally, if a task ID appears as a value string inside another task's params, the search will find it there first, fail the colon check, advance past it, and may miss the actual key occurrence.
- **Impact:** Wrong task block extracted or patched; silent data corruption in generated JCWF.
- **Fix:** Use simdjson to locate task entries rather than textual search.

- **Category:** correctness / exception
- **Location:** `MergeJcwfFragments()`
- **Issue:** The function inserts `additionalTasks` (the inner content of a `"tasks"` object from an AI response) directly into `result` via `result.insert(closePos, insertion)`. If the AI response is malformed — unterminated string, unbalanced braces, trailing comma — the merged result is also malformed JSON. There is no parse/validate step between extraction and insertion.

### 69_doc_application_web_mcpKeyManager_h

<a id="69-doc-application-web-mcpkeymanager-h"></a>

*Source doc:* `../../../queue/jarvisCppSafetyAudit/69_doc_application_web_mcpKeyManager_h/docu.output.md`



### HIGH — TOCTOU / non-atomic file write in `Save`

- **Category:** TOCTOU / resource
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::Save`, approximately lines 290–315
- **Issue:** The file is opened with `std::ios::trunc` directly on the final path. If the process crashes or throws between the `open` and the completion of `file.write`, the destination file is left truncated (zero bytes or partially written). There is no write-to-temp-then-rename pattern.
- **Impact:** On a crash or `ofstream` write error mid-stream, the encrypted key store is silently destroyed. The next `Load` will fail with "file is empty" or a decryption error and all keys are lost.
- **Fix:** Write to a sibling temp path (e.g. `path` + `.tmp`), call `file.flush()` + check `file.good()`, then `std::filesystem::rename(tmpPath, path)`. `rename(2)` is atomic on POSIX for same-filesystem moves. Also check the return value of `file.close()` / stream state after `write`.

---

### HIGH — `Save` ignores write errors; `file.close()` result unchecked

- **Category:** resource / exception
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::Save`, approximately line 309
- **Issue:** After `file.write(...)`, neither the stream's `badbit`/`failbit` nor the result of `file.close()` is tested. On Linux, buffered data can be flushed during `close()` and only then fail (e.g. disk-full). The function returns `true` even if the write silently failed.
- **Impact:** Caller believes the store was saved; the on-disk file contains partial or no data.
- **Fix:** After `file.write`, check `!file.good()`. After `file.close()` (or before if using explicit flush), check `!file` and return `false` with a `LOG_CORE_ERROR`.

---

### HIGH — `SelfRenew` TOCTOU: authenticate-then-lock gap

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::SelfRenew`, approximately lines 385–420
- **Issue:** `Authenticate` is called outside any lock held by `SelfRenew` (it acquires and releases `m_Mutex` internally). Between the time `Authenticate` returns and `SelfRenew` re-acquires `m_Mutex`, another thread can revoke, disable, or delete the key identified by `auth->m_Record.m_KeyId`. The subsequent `FindByKeyIdUnlocked` may then return `nullptr` (handled) or, worse, the key slot could be re-used by a different key with the same ID (theoretically, if IDs collide due to short prefix).
- **Impact:** A revoked key can generate a new valid key if revocation and self-renewal race. In the non-race case the code is merely redundant. The enabled/expiry checks done on the snapshot from `Authenticate` are stale by the time the new key is committed.
- **Fix:** Restructure `SelfRenew` to hold `m_Mutex` for the full authenticate-and-mint operation, or inline the authentication lookup inside the lock (since the helper `FindByKeyIdUnlocked` is already designed for in-lock use).

---

### HIGH — `ActivateEnrollment` does not call `Save`; dangling raw pointer after `m_Keys.push_back`

- **Category:** memory / lifetime
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::ActivateEnrollment`, approximately line 360 (`m_Keys.push_back(rec)`)
- **Issue:** The `Record` returned as `out.m_Record` is a copy of `rec` taken before `push_back`, which is correct. However `FindByKeyIdUnlocked` (and its callers) return raw `Record*` pointers into `m_Keys`. Any `push_back` or `erase` on `m_Keys` (which happens inside `ActivateEnrollment`, `SelfRenew`, `RevokeKey`, `CreateBootstrapAdminKey`) invalidates all existing iterators and pointers into the vector.
- **Impact:** In `SelfRenew`, `oldRec` (a `Record*` from `FindByKeyIdUnlocked`) is held across `m_Keys.push_back(renewed)`. If the vector reallocates, `oldRec` is a dangling pointer; writing to `oldRec->m_ExpiresAt` is undefined behaviour.
- **Fix:** In `SelfRenew`, record the index (not a pointer) of the old key before `push_back`, then index by position after the push. Alternatively use `std::list` or `std::deque` (stable addresses) for `m_Keys`, or do the expiry update after noting the index: `size_t oldIdx = oldRec - m_Keys.data(); m_Keys.push_back(...); m_Keys[oldIdx].m_ExpiresAt = ...`.

---

### MEDIUM — `IsPast` returns `false` on unparseable timestamps; silently permits expired tokens

- **Category:** logging / exception
- **Location:** `IsPast`, approximately line 218; used in `ActivateEnrollment` and `PurgeExpiredEnrollments`
- **Issue:** The comment says "be lenient on unparseable timestamps" and returns `false`, meaning a malformed `expires_at` is treated as not-expired. An enrollment record with a corrupt or empty `m_ExpiresAt` will never be purged and can be activated indefinitely.
- **Impact:** A stored enrollment with a missing or malformed expiry field becomes a permanent enrollment token.
- **Fix:** Treat a missing/unparseable expiry as already expired (return `true`). Add a `LOG_CORE_WARN` so operators can see corrupt records. If "lenient" behaviour is truly required for keys (not enrollments), split the helper into two versions with explicit policies.

---

### MEDIUM — `Authenticate` mutates `rec->m_LastUsedAt` but returns a stale copy of the record

- **Category:** concurrency / correctness
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::Authenticate`, approximately lines 400–415
- **Issue:** The function first copies `*rec` into `out.m_Record`, then updates `rec->m_LastUsedAt`. The returned `out.m_Record.m_LastUsedAt` therefore reflects the value _before_ this call, not after. Callers who inspect the returned record see an inconsistent "last used" time.
- **Impact:** Minor functional incorrectness; `SelfRenew` copies `auth->m_Record` into `renewed` and then clears `renewed.m_LastUsedAt` anyway, but any other consumer of the returned record gets a stale field.
- **Fix:** Update `rec->m_LastUsedAt` before copying into `out.m_Record`, or copy after the update.

---

### MEDIUM — `Load` acquires lock only after decryption; `m_Loaded` visible as `false` during parse

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::Load`, approximately lines 270–285
- **Issue:** `Load` opens the file, reads it, decrypts, and only then acquires `m_Mutex` before calling `ParseFromJson` and setting `m_Loaded = true`. If two threads call `Load` concurrently, both can decrypt and both will call `ParseFromJson`, each clearing and repopulating `m_Keys`/`m_Enrollments` without coordination, leading to a data race on those vectors (one thread reads while another clears).
- **Impact:** Concurrent calls to `Load` race on `m_Keys` and `m_Enrollments`, causing undefined behaviour.
- **Fix:** Either document that `Load` must not be called concurrently (and add an assertion), or acquire the mutex for the full duration including file I/O, or use a separate initialisation flag tested under the lock at entry to `Load`.

---

### MEDIUM — `ParseFromJson` is called with the lock held but modifies `m_Keys`/`m_Enrollments` without exception safety

- **Category:** exception / concurrency
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::ParseFromJson`, approximately lines 520–600
- **Issue:** `ParseFromJson` calls `m_Keys.clear()` and `m_Enrollments.clear()` at entry, then incrementally pushes records. If a `std::bad_alloc` (or any other exception from `push_back` or `ReadString`) is thrown mid-way, `m_Keys` and `m_Enrollments` are left in a partially-populated state while `m_Loaded` may remain `true` from a prior successful load. The lock is held at throw time, which means the mutex is correctly released by RAII — but the data is corrupt.
- **Impact:** After an OOM during `Load`, subsequent calls see a partial key set without any indication of failure.
- **Fix:** Parse into local `std::vector<Record>` and `std::vector<EnrollmentRecord>`, then swap into `m_Keys`/`m_Enrollments` only on complete success. This gives strong exception safety for the parse step.

---

### MEDIUM — `RecordDiskUsage` overwrites rather than accumulates; semantics are unclear

- **Category:** correctness / logging
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::RecordDiskUsage`, approximately line 460
- **Issue:** The function sets `m_DiskUsageByUser[user] = bytes` (assignment). The name "Record" implies additive accumulation; the public comment says "Adhoc disk quota bookkeeping (bytes, keyed by user identity)." If callers pass a delta, the value is always replaced, silently discarding prior usage.
- **Impact:** Quota enforcement based on `GetDiskUsage` will be wrong if any caller passes a delta instead of an absolute total.
- **Fix:** Clarify in the API comment and function signature whether `bytes` is absolute or incremental. If incremental, use `+=`; if absolute, rename to `SetDiskUsage`.

---

### MEDIUM — `CreateEnrollment` validation logs `WARN` for a programmatic precondition violation

- **Category:** logging severity
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::CreateEnrollment`, approximately line 323
- **Issue:** An empty `user` or `role` is a caller contract violation (missing required field). The log uses `LOG_CORE_WARN`. For a condition that will always fail the operation and indicates a programming error or malformed API call, `ERROR` is more appropriate.
- **Impact:** Operators triaging why enrollment creation returned empty string may miss the log at WARN level if their alert threshold is ERROR.
- **Fix:** Change to `LOG_CORE_ERROR`.

---

### MEDIUM — `Authenticate` does not check `rec->m_Enabled` or `rec->m_ExpiresAt`

- **Category:** correctness
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::Authenticate`, approximately lines 400–415
- **Issue:** `Authenticate` returns a successful `AuthResult` even if `rec->m_Enabled == false` or the key is expired (`DaysUntilExpiry < 0`). `SelfRenew` checks `auth->m_Record.m_Enabled` and `auth->m_DaysUntilExpiry` after the fact, but callers who use `Authenticate` directly (e.g., the HTTP handler) must remember to do the same check.
- **Impact:** A disabled or expired key that is not revoked (just flagged) can successfully authenticate on any caller path that forgets the secondary check.
- **Fix:** Either enforce enabled/expiry inside `Authenticate` and return `std::nullopt` for disabled/expired records (cleaner for callers), or document the contract explicitly and add assertions in `SelfRenew` that duplicate checks were intentional.

---

### LOW — `Authenticate` constructs `std::string(kKeyPrefix)` twice for a size computation

- **Category:** C++20 / style
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::Authenticate`, approximately lines 396–398
- **Issue:** `std::string(kKeyPrefix).size()` constructs a heap-allocated `std::string` purely to obtain the length of a string literal. `std::string_view(kKeyPrefix).size()` or `std::strlen(kKeyPrefix)` would be zero-cost.
- **Impact:** Unnecessary allocation on every authentication call (minor performance issue, not a safety bug).
- **Fix:** Use `std::string_view kKeyPrefixSv = kKeyPrefix; kKeyPrefixSv.size()` or simply `sizeof("mcp_") - 1`.

---

### LOW — `FindByKeyIdUnlocked` returns a raw `Record*` into a `std::vector` with no enforcement of the "caller holds lock" contract

- **Category:** rust-equivalent / concurrency
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::FindByKeyIdUnlocked`, approximately lines 480–495
- **Issue:** The convention "caller already holds `m_Mutex`" is documented only in a comment. Nothing prevents a caller from using the returned pointer after releasing the lock, or from calling the function without holding the lock.
- **Impact:** A future maintenance change that calls `FindByKeyIdUnlocked` without the lock causes a data race that is invisible at the call site. In Rust, the borrow checker enforces that a reference derived from a `MutexGuard`-locked value cannot outlive the guard.
- **Fix:** Emulate the Rust guarantee: make `FindByKeyIdUnlocked` a private method that takes `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>&` by const-reference as a parameter. The caller must pass the guard, proving they hold it. The pointer must not be stored past the guard's scope.

---

### LOW — `SelfRenew` hardcodes 90-day expiry instead of reusing the key's original expiry period

- **Category:** correctness
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::SelfRenew`, approximately line 400
- **Issue:** The renewed key always expires in exactly 90 days (`std::chrono::hours(24 * 90)`), regardless of the expiry policy carried by the original `EnrollmentRecord` (which had a configurable `m_KeyExpiryDays`). The `Record` struct itself does not store the original expiry duration, only the absolute timestamp.
- **Impact:** Self-renewal silently changes key lifetime policy; a key originally created with a 30-day expiry gets 90 days on renewal.
- **Fix:** Either store the original `m_KeyExpiryDays` in `Record`, or document clearly that self-renewal always grants 90 days.

---

### LOW — `[[nodiscard]]` missing on all error-returning functions

- **Category:** C++20 / rust-equivalent
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager` public interface, header file throughout
- **Issue:** `Load`, `Save`, `UpdateKey`, `RevokeKey` all return `bool` indicating success or failure. `CreateEnrollment` returns an empty string on failure. None are marked `[[nodiscard]]`. A caller that ignores the return value of `Save` or `Load` gets no compiler diagnostic.
- **Impact:** Silent failure: a caller writes `mgr.Save(path, pw);` and never checks whether the save succeeded. In Rust, a `Result<_, E>` return that is dropped without being inspected triggers a `#[must_use]` warning.
- **Fix:** Annotate all bool-returning and `std::optional`-returning public methods with `[[nodiscard]]`. Annotate `CreateEnrollment` with `[[nodiscard]]` as well.

---

### LOW — `SerializeToJson` is called with lock held but uses `std::ostringstream` which may throw

- **Category:** exception
- **Location:** `McpKeyManager::Save`, approximately line 290; `SerializeToJson` throughout
- **Issue:** `Save` holds `m_Mutex` while calling `SerializeToJson`. `SerializeToJson` performs repeated string concatenation via `std::ostringstream`. If any of those operations throws `std::bad_alloc`, the exception propagates out through the `std::lock_guard` destructor (which correctly releases the mutex), but `Save` has no `try/catch` and the exception propagates to the caller uncaught.
- **Impact:** An OOM during serialisation causes an unhandled exception to escape `Save`; the caller expects a `bool` return.
- **Fix:** Either wrap the body of `Save` in `try/catch(std::exception const& e)` returning `false` with an error log, or mark `Save` as potentially throwing and update all callers accordingly.

---

### LOW — `JsonEscape` uses a fixed-size `char buf[8]` with `snprintf` for control characters

- **Category:** memory
- **Location:** `JsonEscape`, approximately line 245
- **Issue:** `snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), "\\u%04x", ...)` writes at most 7 characters (`

### 70_doc_application_web_webServer_h

<a id="70-doc-application-web-webserver-h"></a>

*Source doc:* `../../../queue/jarvisCppSafetyAudit/70_doc_application_web_webServer_h/docu.output.md`



### [CRITICAL] Dangling raw pointer to `AdhocWorkflowManager` captured in `SetWorkflowRuntimeManager` lambda

- **Category:** lifetime
- **Location:** `WebServer::SetWorkflowRuntimeManager`, approximately the lambda passed to `SetRunTerminalObserver`
- **Issue:** `adhoc = m_AdhocManager.get()` captures a raw pointer to the `AdhocWorkflowManager` owned by `m_AdhocManager` (a `unique_ptr`). If `SetWorkflowRuntimeManager` is called again with a non-null pointer (resetting the observer), or if `m_AdhocManager` is reset/destroyed before the `WorkflowRuntimeManager` stops calling the observer (e.g., during shutdown where WRM is torn down after WebServer), the stored lambda in WRM holds a dangling pointer. The observer is called from the runtime manager's thread when a run terminates.
- **Impact:** Use-after-free on `adhoc->OnRunCompleted(runId)` on any run completion after `WebServer` is destroyed or `m_AdhocManager` is reset.
- **Fix:** Capture a `shared_ptr` or use a `weak_ptr` pattern. Since `m_AdhocManager` is `unique_ptr`, either convert it to `shared_ptr<AdhocWorkflowManager>` and capture `weak_ptr<AdhocWorkflowManager>`, or ensure the observer is cleared from WRM before `m_AdhocManager` is destroyed (explicit `workflowRuntimeManager->SetRunTerminalObserver(nullptr)` in `Stop()` or destructor).
- **Rust-equivalent:** Rust's borrow checker would reject capturing a raw pointer across a thread boundary entirely. The `Fn` closure stored in WRM would need to be `Send + 'static`, forcing the author to use `Arc<Mutex<...>>` or `Weak<...>`, making the lifetime explicit at compile time.

---

### [CRITICAL] Data race: `m_Clients` read outside lock in `DrainPendingBroadcasts` after snapshot copy

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `WebServer::DrainPendingBroadcasts`, the re-validation loop `if (m_Clients.find(client) == m_Clients.end())`
- **Issue:** After releasing `m_Mutex`, the code iterates `clients` (a local snapshot of `m_Clients`) and for each client re-acquires `m_Mutex` to call `m_Clients.find(client)`. Between the snapshot and the re-check, `onclose` can fire on Crow's ASIO thread, call `m_Clients.erase(&conn)`, and then Crow can destroy the `conn` object entirely. The re-check under lock confirms the pointer is no longer in the set, but `client->send_text(safeBatch)` is called without holding the lock. If `onclose` fires between the re-check's `lock` release and `send_text`, the `connection*` is a dangling pointer.
- **Impact:** Use-after-free crash on `send_text` during concurrent disconnect, particularly under load with many clients.
- **Fix:** Either hold `m_Mutex` for the entire send loop (if Crow's `send_text` does not itself acquire any Crow-internal lock that creates deadlock), or use Crow's connection handle mechanism if available. At minimum, do the find-and-send atomically under one lock acquisition: lock, check, send, unlock per client, without the intermediate lock release and re-acquisition.

---

### [CRITICAL] `const_cast` to call non-const mutating method breaks thread safety

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `WebServer::TryMcpAuth`, `const_cast<WebServer*>(this)->RecordAuthFailure(ip)`
- **Issue:** `TryMcpAuth` and `Authenticate` are `const` member functions. `const_cast`-ing `this` and calling `RecordAuthFailure` (which writes to `m_AuthFailures` under `m_RateLimitMutex`) breaks the implicit guarantee that `const` methods are safe to call concurrently. While `RecordAuthFailure` itself acquires a lock, the `const_cast` hides the mutation from the type system. Additionally, `IsRateLimited` is called as `self->IsRateLimited(...)` via the same `const_cast` pattern throughout `Authenticate`. This compiles only because the developer has obscured the mutation; future refactoring of the `const` qualifier or addition of read-only concurrent callers could produce unsynchronized writes.
- **Impact:** The lock is present and correct today, so this is not an immediate race. However, the `const_cast` means the compiler cannot diagnose a future path that omits the lock. It also violates the `const` contract relied upon by callers.
- **Fix:** Remove `const` from `Authenticate`, `TryMcpAuth`, `TrySessionAuth`, `AttachMcpExpiryHeader`, and `CheckAuth`. These functions mutate shared state (rate-limit buckets, auth failure records) and should not be `const`. Mark only truly read-only query functions as `const`.

---

### [HIGH] `CURL*` handle leaked on all error paths in `HandleOAuthCallbackGet`

- **Category:** resource
- **Location:** `WebServer::HandleOAuthCallbackGet`, curl usage block
- **Issue:** `curl = curl_easy_init()` is followed by `curl_easy_setopt(...)` calls and then `curl_easy_perform`. If any early-return path is added between `curl_easy_init` and `curl_easy_cleanup`, the handle leaks. More critically, the `curl_slist* headers` is allocated with `curl_slist_append` and freed with `curl_slist_free_all(headers)` — but only on the success path after `curl_easy_perform`. If `curl_easy_perform` itself is not the only failure path (e.g., if an exception is thrown from the JSON parser after `curl_easy_cleanup`), there is no issue; but the `headers` slist is freed only just before `curl_easy_cleanup`, meaning the code is correct today but fragile. The simdjson `parser.iterate(paddedJson).get(doc)` returning an error causes an early return without `curl_slist_free_all` — wait, actually `curl_easy_cleanup` and `curl_slist_free_all` are both called before the JSON parsing begins. The actual leak risk: if an exception propagates from any of the `curl_easy_setopt` calls (unlikely for libcurl but possible via `std::bad_alloc` on the `std::string responseBody`), `curl_easy_cleanup` is never called.
- **Impact:** Resource leak of a CURL handle on exception paths.
- **Fix:** Wrap the CURL handle in an RAII guard: `struct CurlGuard { CURL* h; ~CurlGuard() { if(h) curl_easy_cleanup(h); } };`. Similarly wrap `curl_slist*`.

---

### [HIGH] `onopen` callback reads `m_Clients` and diagnostic counters after releasing lock, then logs stale values

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `WebServer::RegisterWebSocket`, `.onopen` lambda
- **Issue:** After the `lock_guard` scope ends, `LOG_APP_INFO("WebSocket client connected (total: {}, lifetime: {}, peak: {})", m_Clients.size(), m_WsTotalConnects, m_WsPeakClients)` reads `m_Clients.size()`, `m_WsTotalConnects`, and `m_WsPeakClients` without holding `m_Mutex`. These are all guarded by `m_Mutex` per the in-code comments. A concurrent `onclose` could erase from `m_Clients` between the lock release and the log call.
- **Impact:** Data race on `m_Clients.size()` and the counter members; undefined behaviour. The logged values are also stale/misleading.
- **Fix:** Copy the values to local variables inside the lock scope and log them after: `size_t clients, connects, peak; { lock_guard ...; clients = m_Clients.size(); connects = m_WsTotalConnects; peak = m_WsPeakClients; } LOG_APP_INFO(..., clients, connects, peak);`

---

### [HIGH] `m_ClientCount` atomic/`m_Clients` unordered_set consistency window

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `WebServer::Broadcast`, `WebServer::BroadcastJSON`, `WebServer::EnqueueLogLine` — early-exit on `m_ClientCount.load()`; `onopen`/`onclose` updating both under `m_Mutex`
- **Issue:** `m_ClientCount` is updated inside `m_Mutex` after modifying `m_Clients`. The fast-path check `if (m_ClientCount.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) == 0) return;` in `Broadcast`/`BroadcastJSON`/`EnqueueLogLine` is a racy optimisation: between the atomic load and acquiring `m_Mutex` to push to `m_PendingBroadcasts`, all clients could disconnect (so the broadcast is unnecessary but not harmful). More seriously, in `DrainPendingBroadcasts`, `clients = m_Clients` is a snapshot taken under lock, but `m_ClientCount` may not reflect it if updated by a concurrent `onopen` between the atomic store and the mutex acquire. This is a minor issue since the atomic is only used as a hint.
- **Impact:** Benign over-sends (messages queued when client count drops to zero after the load). Not a correctness bug but the atomic provides no actual linearization guarantee.
- **Fix:** Either remove the `m_ClientCount` atomic and check `m_Clients.empty()` under the lock, or document that the atomic is purely a performance hint with acknowledged false positives. The current mixed use creates a false sense of lock-free correctness.

---

### [HIGH] `std::filesystem::exists()` followed by `open()` TOCTOU in `ServeDashboardIndex` and `HandleWorkflowVersionGetGet`

- **Category:** TOCTOU
- **Location:** `WebServer::ServeDashboardIndex` (~`fs::exists(distIndex)` then `ServeStaticFile`); `WebServer::HandleWorkflowVersionGetGet` (`fs::exists(versionPath)` then `std::ifstream ifs(versionPath)`); `WebServer::HandleWorkflowVersionRestorePost` (same pattern)
- **Issue:** `fs::exists()` is checked and then the file is opened in a separate operation. Another process or thread could delete or replace the file between the two calls.
- **Impact:** For `ServeDashboardIndex`, a deleted file between check and open yields a 500 instead of a 404 (minor). For version-restore, a replaced file could serve unintended content. For the general case this is a low-severity TOCTOU.
- **Fix:** Remove the `exists()` check and instead check whether the `ifstream` opened successfully, returning the appropriate error. `TryReadBinaryFile` already does this correctly — extend the pattern to all direct `ifstream` opens that are preceded by `exists()`.

---

### [HIGH] `HandleAiInterfacesSavePost` writes config file non-atomically

- **Category:** resource / exception
- **Location:** `WebServer::HandleAiInterfacesSavePost`, `std::ofstream ofs(configPath, ...)`
- **Issue:** The config file is opened with `std::ios::trunc`, truncating it immediately. If the write fails partway through (disk full, exception), the config file is left empty or partially written, corrupting the installation's configuration.
- **Impact:** On write failure the config file is destroyed, requiring manual recovery.
- **Fix:** Write to a temp file and `fs::rename` atomically, exactly as `WriteTextFileAtomic` already does for other files in this codebase. Use `WriteTextFileAtomic` or the same pattern here.

---

### [HIGH] `HandleConfigSettingsPut` writes config file non-atomically

- **Category:** resource / exception
- **Location:** `WebServer::HandleConfigSettingsPut`, `std::ofstream ofs(configPath, std::ios::binary | std::ios::trunc)`
- **Issue:** Same as above — truncating write without atomic rename. The `replaceField` in-place string manipulation is also error-prone: if a field appears multiple times in the JSON (comments, duplicate keys), the first occurrence is replaced and subsequent occurrences are left stale.
- **Impact:** Config file corruption on partial write; incorrect field replacement if the config JSON has been hand-edited with duplicate keys.
- **Fix:** Use `WriteTextFileAtomic`. Consider using a proper JSON round-trip rather than string replacement.

---

### [HIGH] `HandleConnectionsSavePost` writes connections file non-atomically

- **Category:** resource / exception
- **Location:** `WebServer::HandleConnectionsSavePost`, `std::ofstream file(connectionsFilePath)`
- **Issue:** Same pattern: `std::ofstream` without atomic rename. No `std::ios::trunc` is specified (default mode, which also truncates), meaning a failed write leaves a corrupt file.
- **Impact:** `connections.json` corruption on partial write.
- **Fix:** Use `WriteTextFileAtomic`.

---

### [HIGH] `ai-write-scripts` WebSocket handler writes files without authentication re-check of the role

- **Category:** concurrency / lifetime
- **Location:** `WebServer::RegisterWebSocket`, `.onmessage` handler, `else if (type == "ai-write-scripts")`
- **Issue:** The WebSocket `.onaccept` verifies that the caller has _any_ valid credential (viewer, operator, or admin). The `ai-write-scripts` message type writes arbitrary content to `scripts/` without re-checking whether the authenticated role is `admin`. A `viewer` or `operator` who holds a valid session cookie can connect to `/ws` (accepted) and then send an `ai-write-scripts` message to write files to disk.
- **Impact:** Privilege escalation: any authenticated user can write scripts to the server filesystem. This is a safety issue (arbitrary disk writes, overwriting production scripts) as much as a security one.
- **Fix:** At the top of the `ai-write-scripts` branch, re-authenticate the connection or store the role at `onopen` time and check it: `if (stored_role != "admin") { send error; return; }`. Since `crow::websocket::connection` has no built-in per-connection state, store a `std::unordered_map<connection*, AuthResult>` updated in `onopen` and cleaned in `onclose`, guarded by `m_Mutex`.

### [HIGH] `SetWorkflowRuntimeManager` captures raw `m_AdhocManager.get()` without checking for re-entrancy

- **Category:** lifetime
- **Location:** `WebServer::SetWorkflowRuntimeManager`
- **Issue:** If `SetWorkflowRuntimeManager` is called a second time (e.g., due to a restart), a new observer lambda is installed that still points to `adhoc` (the same `m_AdhocManager.get()` raw pointer). But the old lambda in the old WRM instance is never cleared. If the old WRM is still alive and calls the old observer after the new WRM is set, this is fine. However, if `m_AdhocManager` is ever reset between calls, the old lambda's `adhoc` pointer is dangling.
- **Impact:** Use-after-free if `m_AdhocManager` is ever reset.
- **Fix:** As above — use `weak_ptr` or ensure observer is explicitly cleared before any reset.

### [MEDIUM] Exception swallowed silently in `HandleWorkflowRunPost` context parsing

- **Category:** logging
- **Location:** `WebServer::HandleWorkflowRunPost`, the `catch(...)` block after simdjson parsing
- **Issue:** The catch block logs at `WARN` and continues with an empty context. This is documented as intentional ("Malformed body is not fatal"), but the log line does not include the `workflowId` in a consistent way and uses `LOG_APP_WARN` without any structured field for monitoring. More critically, the exception message itself is discarded — `catch(...)` catches everything including `std::bad_alloc`, so an OOM during JSON parsing is logged identically to a malformed JSON body.
- **Impact:** OOM during parsing is masked as a user error; hard to diagnose in production.
- **Fix:** Catch `std::exception const& e` separately and log `e.what()`, then catch `...` for truly unknown exceptions. Use `LOG_APP_ERROR` for the unknown-exception path.

### 71_doc_application_web_webSessionManager_h

<a id="71-doc-application-web-websessionmanager-h"></a>

*Source doc:* `../../../queue/jarvisCppSafetyAudit/71_doc_application_web_webSessionManager_h/docu.output.md`



### MEDIUM: `RandomSessionId` failure returns empty string without caller check

- **Category:** logging / exception
- **Location:** `WebSessionManager::Create`, approximately line 85 (cpp)
- **Issue:** `RandomSessionId()` returns `std::string{}` when `RAND_bytes` fails. `Create` does not check for the empty return value and proceeds to insert a session keyed on `""` into `m_Sessions`, returning a `LoginResult` with an empty `m_SessionId`. The caller receives what looks like a valid `LoginResult` and will hand the empty string to the browser as a cookie value.
- **Impact:** All RAND_bytes-failure sessions map to the same key `""`. A second failure overwrites the first. Any caller that does not treat an empty session-id as an error will proceed as though login succeeded. The `LOG_CORE_ERROR` inside `RandomSessionId` is the only signal; the call-site is silent.
- **Fix:** Return `std::optional<LoginResult>` (or throw) from `Create`, and check `s.m_SessionId.empty()` immediately after `RandomSessionId()` returns. Log `LOG_CORE_ERROR` at the call site with enough context (user, role) and return nullopt/throw before touching `m_Sessions`.

---

### MEDIUM: `m_TimeoutHours` read outside the lock in `PurgeExpired`

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `WebSessionManager::PurgeExpired`, approximately lines 117–118 (cpp)
- **Issue:** `idleLimit` is computed from `m_TimeoutHours` *before* `m_Mutex` is acquired. `SetTimeoutHours` writes `m_TimeoutHours` under the lock. On an architecture without sequential consistency (or under the C++ memory model with no synchronization between the two threads), the read of `m_TimeoutHours` on one thread and the write on another are an unsynchronized data race on a plain `int`.
- **Impact:** Data race → undefined behavior per the C++ standard. In practice the value read is almost always coherent, but the race is real and will be reported by ThreadSanitizer.
- **Fix:** Either move both the `now` and `idleLimit` computations inside the lock, or make `m_TimeoutHours` `std::atomic<int>`. The simplest correct fix is to move the two lines inside the `lock_guard` scope.

---

### LOW: `[[nodiscard]]` missing on `Create` and `Validate`

- **Category:** rust-equivalent / C++20
- **Location:** `WebSessionManager::Create` and `WebSessionManager::Validate` declarations, header ~lines 62–68
- **Issue:** Both functions return values that callers must inspect. `Create` returns the session id that must be sent to the browser; `Validate` returns `std::optional<Session>` whose presence/absence must be checked before serving the request. Neither is marked `[[nodiscard]]`.
- **Impact:** A caller that writes `manager.Create(user, role);` or `manager.Validate(cookie);` without using the result silently discards it. In Rust, `Result<T,E>` and types marked `#[must_use]` produce a compiler warning when their return value is dropped; C++ has the equivalent `[[nodiscard]]` attribute. Without it the compiler emits no diagnostic.
- **Fix:** Add `[[nodiscard]]` to both function declarations in the header. If `Create` is changed to return `std::optional<LoginResult>` (per the finding above), `[[nodiscard]]` becomes even more important.

---

### LOW: `Validate` copies the entire `Session` struct unnecessarily

- **Category:** move / C++20
- **Location:** `WebSessionManager::Validate`, last `return` statement, approximately line 112 (cpp)
- **Issue:** `return it->second;` copies the `Session` value out of the map while the lock is held. The struct contains three `std::string` members and two `time_point` members. A copy is required because the iterator must remain valid only for the duration of the locked section, but the copy could instead be expressed as `return std::move(it->second)` — except that would leave a moved-from session in the map, which is wrong. The real concern is purely allocator overhead and clarity; there is no use-after-free here, but the copy is sometimes written as `std::move` incorrectly by maintainers who then introduce a dangling session.
- **Impact:** Low: unnecessary heap allocation for three strings on every validated request. More importantly, a future maintainer may incorrectly apply `std::move` here and leave a zombie entry.
- **Fix:** The copy is semantically correct as written. Add a comment explaining *why* `std::move` must not be used here. If `Session` becomes large, consider storing a snapshot of only the fields the caller needs rather than the whole struct.

---

### LOW: `GetTimeoutHours` locks a `mutable` mutex in a `const` member function — justify or demote

- **Category:** const / concurrency
- **Location:** `WebSessionManager::GetTimeoutHours`, approximately line 135 (cpp); `m_Mutex` declared `mutable` in header
- **Issue:** `m_Mutex` is `mutable` so that `const` member functions can lock it, which is the standard pattern for logical constness. The issue is that `m_TimeoutHours` itself is not `const` and is written by `SetTimeoutHours`. If `m_TimeoutHours` were `std::atomic<int>` the `mutable` mutex would not be needed for this accessor at all, and the race identified above would be resolved simultaneously.
- **Impact:** Low on its own; mainly a design observation. The combination of `mutable std::mutex` + a plain `int` that is also read outside the lock (PurgeExpired) is the source of the medium-severity race above.
- **Fix:** Change `int m_TimeoutHours` to `std::atomic<int> m_TimeoutHours{8}`. Remove the lock from `GetTimeoutHours` and from the read in `PurgeExpired`. Retain the lock in `SetTimeoutHours` only if a memory-order stronger than `relaxed` is needed, or use `m_TimeoutHours.store(…, std::memory_order_relaxed)` / `load(…, std::memory_order_relaxed)` since the value is advisory and a torn read cannot occur on an `int`-sized atomic.

---

### LOW: No `static_assert` or exhaustive check on `Session` fields after `erase` in `Validate`

- **Category:** rust-equivalent
- **Location:** `WebSessionManager::Validate`, approximately line 107 (cpp)
- **Issue:** When a session is found but expired, `m_Sessions.erase(it)` silently removes it and returns `std::nullopt`. There is no log line recording *why* validation failed (expired vs. unknown). From an operational standpoint, distinguishing "never existed" from "existed but timed out" is useful for detecting session-fixation attempts or misconfigured timeout values. This is a logging-completeness gap, not a crash risk.
- **Impact:** Operators cannot distinguish normal session expiry from unexpected invalidation without adding instrumentation.
- **Fix:** Add a `LOG_CORE_DEBUG` (or `LOG_CORE_INFO`) line on the expiry branch: `"WebSessionManager: session expired for user={} idle={}s"` before the erase. In Rust, the equivalent would be a `match` arm that forces explicit handling of each `Option` branch; in C++, a comment or log on every `return std::nullopt` path serves the same documentary function.

### 72_doc_application_workflow_adhocWorkflowManager_h

<a id="72-doc-application-workflow-adhocworkflowmanager-h"></a>

*Source doc:* `../../../queue/jarvisCppSafetyAudit/72_doc_application_workflow_adhocWorkflowManager_h/docu.output.md`



### [HIGH] Quota pre-check races with disk-usage update

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::Stage`, approximately where `WouldExceedQuota` is called before `std::lock_guard lock(m_Mutex)` is acquired
- **Issue:** `WouldExceedQuota` calls `GetUserDiskUsageBytes`, which acquires `m_Mutex` and releases it, then returns. `Stage` then acquires `m_Mutex` again to proceed with staging. Between the two lock acquisitions another concurrent `Stage` call can pass the quota check simultaneously, and both proceed to stage runs, collectively exceeding the quota.
- **Impact:** Two concurrent requests from the same user can each observe the current usage as within quota and both commit, potentially doubling the effective quota.
- **Fix:** Move the `WouldExceedQuota` check inside the single `lock_guard` scope in `Stage`, so the read and the subsequent write to `m_DiskUsageByUser` are atomic with respect to each other. Inline the check against `m_DiskUsageByUser` directly rather than calling through the locking accessor.

---

### [HIGH] `MeasureFolderBytes` and `ReadMeta` called inside `m_Mutex` lock in `OnRunCompleted`

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::OnRunCompleted`, inside the `std::lock_guard lock(m_Mutex)` block
- **Issue:** `MeasureFolderBytes` performs a recursive filesystem walk and `WriteMeta`/`WriteManifest` do blocking I/O, all while `m_Mutex` is held. Any other caller of `Stage`, `GetActiveRunCount`, `GetRunInfo`, `GetUserDiskUsageBytes`, or `Reap` will block for the entire duration of those filesystem operations.
- **Impact:** Thread contention: a slow filesystem or large output tree causes every other API call to stall for an unbounded time. `Reap` also holds `m_Mutex` while calling `ReadMeta` and `MeasureFolderBytes` for the same reason.
- **Fix:** Snapshot only the metadata needed (folder path, user, policy, existing byte count) under the lock, release it, do all filesystem I/O outside the lock, then re-acquire to update the maps.

---

### [HIGH] `Reap` holds `m_Mutex` during filesystem directory walk

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::Reap`, the `std::lock_guard lock(m_Mutex)` scope that wraps the entire `directory_iterator` loop
- **Issue:** The full two-level directory scan (`directory_iterator` over `m_BasePath` and inner `directory_iterator` over each user-slug dir) runs while `m_Mutex` is held. Filesystem iteration can block on slow media, NFS, or when the directory is large.
- **Impact:** Every caller that needs `m_Mutex` (Stage, OnRunCompleted, GetRunInfo, all query methods) is blocked for the duration of the scan. If the scan itself throws (and the `try`/`catch` is in `ReaperLoop`, not here), the mutex is unlocked via `lock_guard` RAII, but the `toDelete` vector is then used without the lock, which is safe; however the blocking is still a liveness problem.
- **Fix:** Collect paths under the lock using only in-memory data (`m_RunIdToMeta` keys already have the folder paths), or do the directory scan outside the lock and only lock briefly to look up deletion candidates.

---

### [HIGH] `RemoveFolder` called in `Reap` after releasing `m_Mutex`, but `ReadMeta`/`MeasureFolderBytes` also happen outside the lock — TOCTOU with `OnRunCompleted`

- **Category:** TOCTOU
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::Reap`, lines that call `ReadMeta(folder)` and `MeasureFolderBytes(folder)` and then `RemoveFolder(folder)` after the lock is released, interleaved with a second `std::lock_guard lock(m_Mutex)` for the map update
- **Issue:** After the outer `m_Mutex` lock is released, `OnRunCompleted` may concurrently find the same run, call `RemoveFolder` for `on_completion` policy, and erase it from `m_RunIdToMeta`. The reaper then calls `ReadMeta` and `MeasureFolderBytes` on a folder that no longer exists, and subsequently tries to `RemoveFolder` a path already deleted. The second `lock_guard` in the reaper's loop then double-decrements `m_DiskUsageByUser` via `m_RunIdToMeta.erase` on a key already erased.
- **Impact:** `m_DiskUsageByUser` underflows (wraps around since `size_t` is unsigned) producing a huge usage figure that permanently blocks staging for that user.
- **Fix:** Check that the run folder still exists (with `std::error_code`) before acting on it outside the lock, and check that the `m_RunIdToMeta` entry still exists before decrementing usage inside the second lock acquisition. Alternatively, consolidate removal into a single locked critical section using only in-memory state.

---

### [MEDIUM] `m_Counter` fetch_add races with `m_Mutex`-protected folder name generation

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::GenerateFolderName`, called from `Stage` while `m_Mutex` is held; `m_Counter` is `std::atomic<uint32_t>` but `Iso8601NowCompactUtc()` is called separately
- **Issue:** The timestamp and the counter are sampled in two separate steps. Two concurrent `Stage` calls that both hold `m_Mutex` sequentially will get different counters but could theoretically get the same timestamp if the clock resolution is coarse (second-granular). More importantly, `GenerateFolderName` is called inside `Stage`'s lock, but `m_Counter.fetch_add` is also callable from outside the lock (e.g., a hypothetical future caller), making the atomicity of counter vs. timestamp non-guaranteed. Currently the combination is unique only because `Stage` serialises via `m_Mutex`, making the atomic on `m_Counter` redundant and misleading about the actual synchronisation model.
- **Impact:** Future refactors removing the mutex scope around `GenerateFolderName` will silently break uniqueness guarantees.
- **Fix:** Either remove the `atomic` and document that `GenerateFolderName` must be called under `m_Mutex`, or make counter increment the only uniqueness mechanism and drop the timestamp from the uniqueness contract.

---

### [MEDIUM] `WriteMeta` failure is silently ignored in `Stage`

- **Category:** logging
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::Stage`, call to `WriteMeta(folder, meta)`
- **Issue:** `WriteMeta` opens the file with `std::ofstream` and returns early without logging or returning an error if the open fails (`if (!os) return;`). `Stage` does not check any return value from `WriteMeta`. If `meta.json` is never written, `ReadMeta` in `Init` or `Reap` will return `std::nullopt` for that run, causing disk-usage attribution to be lost on restart and the reaper to be unable to decrement usage correctly on deletion.
- **Impact:** Disk-usage accounting silently goes wrong on restart; the error is completely invisible.
- **Fix:** Change `WriteMeta` to return `bool` (or `std::string` error), mark it `[[nodiscard]]`, log a `LOG_APP_ERROR` on failure with `runId`/`user` in scope, and have `Stage` treat a `WriteMeta` failure as a staging failure (remove the folder and return an error string).

---

### [MEDIUM] `WriteManifest` failure silently ignored in `OnRunCompleted`

- **Category:** logging
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::OnRunCompleted`, call to `WriteManifest`; `WriteManifest` itself returns early with `if (!os) return`
- **Issue:** Same pattern as `WriteMeta`: if the manifest file cannot be opened, `WriteManifest` returns silently with no log. `OnRunCompleted` does not check a return value.
- **Impact:** Downstream listing/download endpoints that depend on `manifest.json` will find it absent without any indication of why.
- **Fix:** `WriteManifest` should return `bool`, be `[[nodiscard]]`, log `LOG_APP_ERROR` on failure with `runId` in scope, and `OnRunCompleted` should log the error.

---

### [MEDIUM] Filesystem walk in `MeasureFolderBytes` silently stops on first error

- **Category:** exception / resource
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::MeasureFolderBytes`
- **Issue:** The loop breaks on the first `ec` error from the iterator (`if (ec) break`), returning whatever partial sum was accumulated. No log is emitted. If a permission error or I/O error occurs partway through the walk, the returned size is silently under-reported.
- **Impact:** Quota accounting underestimates disk usage; users may be allowed to stage more runs than the quota allows.
- **Fix:** Log `LOG_APP_WARN` or `LOG_APP_ERROR` when `ec` is set, and consider whether partial results should be returned or an error should be propagated.

---

### [MEDIUM] `ReaperLoop` stop condition has a data race on `m_ReaperRunning` with `StopReaperThread`

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::StopReaperThread` and `AdhocWorkflowManager::ReaperLoop`
- **Issue:** `StopReaperThread` calls `m_ReaperThread.join()` after setting `m_ReaperRunning` to `false`. The destructor calls `StopReaperThread`. If `StartReaperThread` is called after `StopReaperThread` has set `m_ReaperRunning = false` but before `join()` completes, `m_ReaperRunning.exchange(true)` in `StartReaperThread` will return `false` (as if not running), spawning a second thread into `m_ReaperThread` while the first thread is still alive and being joined. This overwrites `m_ReaperThread` before the old one is joined, causing `std::terminate` or UB.
- **Impact:** In practice this is a misuse-of-API risk rather than an internal bug, but the destructor path (`~AdhocWorkflowManager` → `StopReaperThread`) is always exercised, and any external call to `StartReaperThread` after destruction has begun is undefined.
- **Fix:** Add a condition variable or a dedicated stop flag + notify mechanism; or document that `StartReaperThread`/`StopReaperThread` are not re-entrant and assert `!m_ReaperThread.joinable()` in `StartReaperThread`.

---

### [MEDIUM] `file_time_type` clock conversion in `WriteManifest` is non-portable and potentially imprecise

- **Category:** C++20
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::WriteManifest`, mtime conversion block
- **Issue:** The code converts `std::filesystem::file_time_type` to `std::chrono::system_clock::time_point` via the arithmetic `ftime - file_time_type::clock::now() + system_clock::now()`. This is the pre-C++20 workaround. Under C++20, `std::chrono::clock_cast` is available and correct. The subtraction of two `now()` calls introduces a race window: if significant time passes between the two `now()` calls, or if the clocks tick at different rates, the computed time will be wrong. On some platforms `file_time_type::clock` is not `system_clock`.
- **Impact:** File modification timestamps in `manifest.json` may be off by the scheduling jitter between the two `now()` calls, or wrong by a constant offset on platforms where the clocks differ.
- **Fix:** Under C++20 use `std::chrono::clock_cast<std::chrono::system_clock>(ftime)` directly.

---

### [MEDIUM] `Init` holds `m_Mutex` for the entire directory scan and `MeasureFolderBytes` calls

- **Category:** concurrency
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::Init`, `std::lock_guard lock(m_Mutex)` wraps the full scan including `ReadMeta` and `MeasureFolderBytes` for every run folder
- **Issue:** `Init` is documented as a startup function, so no other thread should be active yet; however there is no enforcement of this. If `StartReaperThread` or `Stage` is called concurrently with `Init` (e.g. from another thread in the HTTP server startup), they will block for the full scan duration or, worse, observe partially-initialised state before the scan completes.
- **Impact:** Liveness issue during startup; no crash, but potential for quota undercount if `Stage` races past an incomplete scan.
- **Fix:** Document that `Init` must be called before any other method and before any threads are started, and add an `assert(!m_ReaperRunning)` guard. Alternatively, use a separate initialisation flag checked by all other methods.

---

### [LOW] `GenerateFolderName` format string truncation for counter over 9999

- **Category:** memory
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::GenerateFolderName`
- **Issue:** `counterBuf[8]` and `snprintf(counterBuf, sizeof(counterBuf), "%04u", counter)` — `uint32_t` max is 4,294,967,295 (10 digits). Once the counter exceeds 9999 the format still fits in the buffer (10 digits + null = 11 > 8). `snprintf` will truncate silently, writing 7 characters plus a null, producing folder names with a truncated counter string.
- **Impact:** Folder names become non-unique once counter ≥ 10,000,000, potentially colliding. `create_directories` will fail on collision; the error is returned to the caller.
- **Fix:** Increase `counterBuf` to at least 12 bytes, or use `std::to_string(counter)` with `std::string::insert` for zero-padding.

---

### [LOW] `SanitizeUserSlug` returns empty string for all-non-ASCII input, but caller treats empty slug as hard error only partially

- **Category:** logging
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::Stage`, after `SanitizeUserSlug`
- **Issue:** An all-non-ASCII `req.m_User` produces a slug that is empty (every byte fails the allowed-character test). `Stage` returns `"invalid_user_for_staging"` with no log. The condition `userSlug.empty()` is checked, but since every non-ASCII character is mapped to `'_'` (which is in the allowed set), the slug will actually never be empty for a non-empty `user`. The empty-slug check is therefore dead code, but it would be reachable if the allowed-character set were ever tightened.
- **Impact:** No current runtime impact; dead guard causes confusion.
- **Fix:** Add a `LOG_APP_WARN` or `LOG_APP_ERROR` at the dead guard so that if the condition ever becomes reachable it is visible; or remove it and assert instead.

---

### [LOW] `ReadMeta` JSON parser is vulnerable to fields embedded in values

- **Category:** memory / correctness
- **Location:** `AdhocWorkflowManager::ReadMeta`, `pluck` lambda
- **Issue:** The parser searches for `"field"` as a substring anywhere in the file content. If any field value itself contains a string that looks like a JSON key (e.g., a user string containing `"cleanup_policy"`), the pluck for a subsequent field will find the occurrence inside the value of an earlier field and return a wrong result. The file is written by the same code and values go through `JsonEscape`, but the parser does not use the escaping to verify boundaries.
- **Impact:** In the general case, misread metadata leads to wrong user attribution, wrong cleanup policy, or wrong owner_slug — causing quota miscounting or failed authorisation checks. In practice the written values are constrained, but this is a correctness fragility.
- **Fix:** Use a proper JSON parser (nlohmann/json or similar already used elsewhere in the project per the includes), or at minimum anchor the search to start from the top-level object rather than re-scanning from the beginning for each field.

### 74_doc_application_workflow_aiCallTaskExecutor_h

<a id="74-doc-application-workflow-aicalltaskexecutor-h"></a>

*Source doc:* `../../../queue/jarvisCppSafetyAudit/74_doc_application_workflow_aiCallTaskExecutor_h/docu.output.md`



### [HIGH] `onReply` lambda captures `requestPool` raw pointer and `taskWorkingDirectoryPath` by value after potential task teardown

- **Category:** lifetime
- **Location:** `AiCallTaskExecutor::Execute`, the `onReply` lambda constructed inside the chunked fan-out loop, approximately where `auto onReply = [aggregator, chunkIndex, totalChunks, writeConcatFallback](...)`
- **Issue:** `requestPool` is a raw pointer obtained from `app->GetAiRequestPool()` and stored inside `ChunkAggregator::m_RequestPool`. The `ChunkAggregator` is kept alive by a `shared_ptr` that is captured in async callbacks. However, `requestPool` itself is a raw pointer whose owner (`JarvisAgent`/`AiRequestPool`) can be destroyed while an in-flight AI reply callback still holds and dereferences it via `agg->m_RequestPool->OnOutputFileCreated(...)` or `agg->m_RequestPool->Submit(...)`. There is no `weak_ptr` or lifetime fence. Similarly, `writeConcatFallback` is captured by value into `onReply`, which is itself captured into `onReply` — this is a recursive capture that compiles only because both lambdas copy the `shared_ptr`, but the raw `m_RequestPool` inside `ChunkAggregator` has no lifetime coupling to the pool's actual owner.
- **Impact:** If the engine is shut down or the pool is destroyed while a chunk reply is still outstanding, `agg->m_RequestPool->OnOutputFileCreated(...)` dereferences a dangling pointer, causing undefined behaviour (crash or silent data corruption).
- **Fix:** Store `std::weak_ptr<AiRequestPool>` (or an equivalent `std::weak_ptr` to the owning object) inside `ChunkAggregator` instead of a raw pointer. At callback time, lock the weak pointer and bail out if it has expired. Alternatively, wrap `AiRequestPool` in a `shared_ptr` and share ownership into all async callbacks. This is the C++ equivalent of Rust's `Weak<T>` / `Arc<T>` split that the borrow checker would enforce.

### [HIGH] `writeConcatFallback` lambda captures `writeConcatFallback` itself by copy (recursive std::function capture not done; worse, it is a non-capturing generic lambda copied into `onReply`)

- **Category:** lifetime
- **Location:** `AiCallTaskExecutor::Execute`, chunked fan-out, `writeConcatFallback` definition and its capture inside `onReply`
- **Issue:** `writeConcatFallback` is a local lambda defined with `auto const writeConcatFallback = [...]`. It is then immediately captured by value into `onReply` as `[aggregator, chunkIndex, totalChunks, writeConcatFallback]`. Because `writeConcatFallback` is a lambda (not a `std::function`), the copy inside `onReply` is a copy of the closure object. This is technically safe in terms of copying, but `onReply` itself is then passed to `requestPool->Submit(chunkEnvelope, onReply)`. The signature of `Submit` almost certainly takes `std::function<void(AiReply const&)>` or similar. If `Submit` stores the callback and later dispatches it on a different thread, the copied `writeConcatFallback` closure (which itself holds a copy of `aggregator` shared_ptr) is fine for data, but the outer `taskWorkingDirectoryPath`, `stngTaskPrefix`, `probContent`, `probRelativeName`, and `stngTaskPrefix` variables are all stack-allocated locals in `Execute`. `writeConcatFallback` does NOT capture any of those directly — it receives `agg` by the shared_ptr and reads `agg->m_QueueFolder` etc., which are stored inside the aggregator. This part is safe. However, the `onReply` lambda also captures `stngTaskPrefix`, `probContent` (both by implicit copy via the `[aggregator, chunkIndex, totalChunks, writeConcatFallback]` capture list — actually it does NOT capture those since they are not listed). Re-reading: `onReply` only captures `aggregator`, `chunkIndex`, `totalChunks`, `writeConcatFallback`. All are by value. This sub-issue is resolved, but the real risk is that `chunkEnvelope.m_Messages` holds a `std::string` moved-from `chunkBody`, and the `onReply` registered with each `Submit` call indexes into `aggregator->m_Parts[chunkIndex]` — the chunkIndex is captured by value at the correct iteration value only if the lambda copy happens before the next loop iteration increments the index. Because `chunkIndex` is captured by value, this is safe. Revising: the actual HIGH issue here is `aggregator->m_RequestPool` raw pointer as described above.

- **Impact:** (Subsumes into the finding above; this entry is retracted as a distinct HIGH.) See finding above.
- **Fix:** See finding above.
